content: For non-ulcerative lesions, it is essential to obtain a fine-needle aspirate from the estimated center of the lesion prior to initiating antibiotic therapy. This sample should be subjected to microbiological analysis, including direct smear examination, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and culture. If histopathological analysis is deemed necessary, alternative methods such as punch or surgical biopsy may be employed. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides specific guidance on specimen collection for laboratory confirmation. Differential diagnoses for such lesions include tropical phagedenic ulcer, necrotizing fasciitis, venous ulcers (particularly in older individuals), diabetic ulcers, ulcers associated with sickle-cell disease, yaws, cutaneous tuberculosis, leprosy, cutaneous leishmaniasis, and malignant skin ulcers. The recommended antibiotic regimen for Buruli ulcer involves a combination of rifampicin with either clarithromycin or moxifloxacin. For individuals living with HIV who are initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), a dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimen is preferred. However, due to pharmacokinetic interactions between rifampicin and DTG, the DTG dose should be increased to 50 mg twice daily when these drugs are used concurrently. The same principles apply to alternative first-line and second-line ART regimens for people with HIV who do not have Buruli ulcer disease. Clarithromycin and efavirenz (EFV) interact in a way that significantly reduces clarithromycin levels, potentially diminishing its efficacy and increasing the risk of toxicity, such as skin rash. Therefore, caution is advised when combining rifampicin and clarithromycin with EFV. Protease inhibitors (PIs) are also significantly reduced in concentration when used with rifampicin and should be avoided during Buruli ulcer treatment. If a patient is already on a PI-based regimen, it is recommended to switch to DTG with appropriate dose adjustments. Collaboration with tuberculosis (TB) programs is crucial, particularly in areas such as drug procurement coordination, laboratory network utilization, and monitoring for antibiotic resistance. Similarly, collaboration with HIV/AIDS programs is essential for managing individuals with Buruli ulcer who may also be living with HIV. Establishing a network of laboratories capable of high-performance PCR-based diagnosis of Buruli ulcer is critical in endemic African regions. For individuals co-infected with Buruli ulcer and HIV, high-quality facility-based HIV testing and counseling should be offered. Antibiotic treatment for Buruli ulcer should commence before starting ART and should be administered for eight weeks. The recommended antibiotic combination is rifampicin plus clarithromycin, with dose adjustments for DTG due to drug-drug interactions with rifampicin. An alternative regimen is rifampicin plus moxifloxacin. Rapid ART initiation is recommended for all individuals co-infected with Buruli ulcer and HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Screening for TB should be conducted before initiating Buruli ulcer treatment and ART. Those with advanced HIV disease should receive a comprehensive care package, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and adherence support interventions. Programs should implement monitoring and reporting systems to evaluate the outcomes of Buruli ulcer and HIV interventions. Leishmaniasis is a group of diseases caused by Leishmania species, transmitted through the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. The three main forms are visceral (kala-azar), cutaneous, and mucocutaneous. It disproportionately affects poor and marginalized populations with limited access to healthcare. In 2018, over 95% of new cases reported to WHO occurred in 10 countries, including Brazil, India, and Sudan. While only a fraction of those infected develop the disease, an estimated 700,000 to 1 million new cases occur annually. The burden of visceral leishmaniasis among people living with HIV has increased in recent decades. Visceral leishmaniasis is a significant opportunistic infection associated with HIV in certain regions. The two diseases are mutually reinforcing, with HIV increasing susceptibility to visceral leishmaniasis and the latter accelerating HIV replication and disease progression. HIV co-infection increases the risk of developing active visceral leishmaniasis by 100 to 2320 times. In endemic areas, many individuals have asymptomatic infections. Since 1985, 42 countries have reported cases of HIV and leishmaniasis co-infection. In southern Europe, up to 70% of visceral leishmaniasis cases among adults are associated with HIV, although the number of new cases has declined due to improved ART access. The clinical presentation of visceral leishmaniasis in people living with HIV is often atypical, involving various organs such as the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and skin, particularly in those with advanced HIV disease or low CD4 cell counts. Co-infection with other opportunistic infections is common, complicating early diagnosis. Cases of visceral leishmaniasis have been reported in association with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) among individuals with latent Leishmania infection or those previously treated for visceral leishmaniasis who are receiving ART. Diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis relies on positive parasitology (e.g., stained smears from bone marrow or spleen) and/or serology (e.g., ELISA, rK39, or PCR). For HIV co-infected individuals, diagnostic tests perform less effectively, with lower sensitivity and specificity. Parasite loads are higher, and parasites may be found in unusual sites. WHO recommends liposomal amphotericin B combined with miltefosine as the preferred treatment regimen for visceral leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection in eastern Africa and South-East Asia. Secondary prophylaxis after the first episode is advised to reduce relapse risk. Optimal management aims to cure visceral leishmaniasis and achieve undetectable HIV viral loads through rapid ART initiation. For pregnant individuals, treatment options are limited. Amphotericin B formulations are considered the safest, with no reported cases of abortion or vertical transmission among those treated with liposomal amphotericin B. However, miltefosine, part of the combination regimen, is potentially embryotoxic and teratogenic and should not be used during pregnancy. Experts recommend maintaining a pregnancy registry to evaluate drug fetotoxicity. Visceral leishmaniasis diagnostics and medicines must be continuously available, affordable, and accessible. Coordination between leishmaniasis and HIV programs is essential for effective management. Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide, with an estimated 500,000 new cases in 2018. Over 311,000 women die annually from cervical cancer, with 87% of deaths occurring in lowand middle-income countries. Women living with HIV have a six-fold higher risk of cervical cancer than those without HIV. Cervical cancer is classified as an AIDS-defining condition. This increased risk is due to a higher likelihood of acquiring HPV infection, lower regression rates of pre-cancer lesions, faster progression to cancer, and higher recurrence rates after treatment. ART has significantly reduced AIDS-related mortality and increased life expectancy, with over 19 million women living with HIV globally in 2019. Following a WHO call to action in 2018, 194 countries committed to eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. The 2030 targets include vaccinating 90% of girls with the HPV vaccine by age 15, screening 70% of women with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and ensuring 90% of women with cervical disease receive treatment. WHO's 2021 guidelines on cervical cancer prevention include 14 new recommendations for women living with HIV. Screening aims to detect precancerous lesions for early treatment. Women living with HIV should have clinical appointments at least every six months, providing opportunities for cervical cancer screening and treatment interventions.
